analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers meal, rest, restroom, and paid medical breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have mandated meal and paid rest breaks for all workers covered by federal wage law, never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a section to the Fair Labor Standards Act, the main federal wage law, which today sets no general requirement for worker breaks. It would require employers to give a 30-minute meal break for every 6 hours worked, a 10-minute paid rest break (or enough time to reach a restroom) for every 4 hours, and up to 20-minute paid breaks for medical needs. Breaks where the worker is not fully relieved of duties would be paid at time-and-a-half, workers could not be forced to waive meal breaks, and stronger state laws and union contracts would stay in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act — including retail, food service, warehouse, and call-center workers, many of whom today work under no federal right to any break. Workers with medical conditions would gain a right to short paid breaks, and workers kept on duty during breaks would get time-and-a-half pay for that time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers with no guaranteed breaks

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to provide a meal break of at least 30 minutes for each 6-hour work period, and could not compel workers to give it up [S2].
Employers would have to provide, during every 4-hour work period, a break of at least 10 minutes or enough time to use the nearest functioning restroom, paid at the regular rate [S2].
Workers could take paid medical breaks of up to 20 minutes each when reasonably required by a medical condition, communicated by the worker or a health care provider [S2].
If an employee is not fully relieved of work duties or cannot leave the site during a meal break, the employer must pay for the whole break at one-and-a-half times the regular rate [S2].
The bill would be enforceable under the Fair Labor Standards Act's existing violation and penalty provisions, and would not override union contracts or state laws with stronger protections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of hourly workers — retailers, restaurants, warehouses, call centers, and other businesses that pay by the hour — would bear the cost of paid rest and medical breaks and of running schedules that allow meal breaks. Small businesses with thin margins and continuous-coverage operations would face the largest adjustments.

drawbacks.text: Paid rest and medical breaks raise labor costs directly; employers would pay for time not spent working, and businesses with tight margins or continuous coverage would face the biggest scheduling and payroll adjustments [S2].

The bill allows an uncompensated meal break when the worker is fully relieved of duties, so a worker's take-home pay for a shift would be slightly lower than under continuous pay — the trade the bill makes for guaranteeing the break itself [S2].

A good-faith objection is that a federal break mandate is blunt: states like California already have detailed break laws, and a one-size federal rule could complicate operations for multistate employers and impose compliance burdens on small businesses even where local rules already cover workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a guaranteed right to eat, rest, and use the restroom during a shift — is real for the large share of the workforce that has no such right under federal law, and the bill preserves stronger state laws and union contracts rather than weakening them. The costs are genuine but conventional: paid break time is a payroll cost employers would absorb through margins, prices, or staffing, and the bill's time-and-a-half rule for interrupted breaks is designed to make skipping breaks expensive rather than free. The main design criticism is the lack of small-business flexibility, not the direction of the policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2024, sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Worker Rights and Support Act in the House on June 28, 2024 [S1] [S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S4].
Thirty-seven Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S3].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of hourly workers, who would have had to provide paid rest and medical breaks and guarantee meal periods, are better off because the bill never moved. Workers gained nothing; the right to take a meal or restroom break remains a matter of state law or employer policy.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Worker Rights and Support Act on June 28, 2024, to add federal meal, rest, restroom, and medical break requirements to the Fair Labor Standards Act.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 37 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats — and the Republican-run committee that controlled the bill's fate never acted on it; no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Hourly-work employers (retail, food service, warehousing, call centers)
industries.note: These employers would have to build paid rest and medical breaks into every shift, guarantee meal periods, and pay time-and-a-half whenever a worker is kept on duty during a break. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs directly against workers' interest in guaranteed breaks, which is why the break mandate never reached the floor.

The bill explicitly does not override collective bargaining agreements, so existing union contracts stand, and unions could negotiate beyond the federal floor. Workers covered by strong contracts would see little change; the bill mainly raises the floor for nonunion workers.
